finding: The site has no live range for this job, so there is nothing to grade; these are first figures. Shops usually sell a coolant service at a set menu price, not as parts plus clocked labor, so the built totals are a floor-to-middle view. They are for a plain drain and refill with the maker's coolant; a machine exchange or a chemical flush costs more. Built totals (coolant + stated hours x $120-$160/hr, the national middle labor rate used for these checks): economy 2015 Corolla about $126-$297 (2 gallons of premix for a 5.8 qt system); midsize 2016 Accord about $122-$285 (2 gallons for a 1.72 gal change); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $113-$268 (1 gallon of concentrate for a 7-7.6 liter system; the BMW comes out lowest only because concentrate goes twice as far, and its bleeding procedure tends to push labor to the upper end). Truck 2016 F-150 5.0L: parts are null, so no total; labor alone is about $90-$240. The coolant type (Motorcraft Orange prediluted VC-3DIL-B) was confirmed in the owner's manual, but the 5.0L capacity could not be read on any page that loaded and no dealer list price was found. For scale only, a marketplace listing showed VC-3DIL-B at $35.59 a gallon and a forum thread cites 17 quarts for the earlier 2013 5.0L, which would mean a truck costs noticeably more in coolant than a car; neither figure is good enough to build on. Against the benchmarks: the built totals cover Jerry's drain-and-fill figure ($80-$150), Jerry's average ($173-$184), Kelley Blue Book ($131-$209) and Capital One's chain-shop range ($175-$250). FIXD's $98-$123 is at or below our floor and looks like labor only. YourMechanic ($301-$337) and RepairPal ($440-$512) are above our tops; RepairPal's parts figure of about $285 is far more than coolant costs ($23-$57 here), so it likely covers more than fluid. A fair plain-language range for a car is roughly $120-$300, higher for trucks and for a machine flush. How solid the numbers are: the labor time is one general statement of 45-90 minutes from a guide co-written by two mechanics, backed by a 30-60 minute do-it-yourself guide; neither is vehicle-specific or a flat-rate book time. No Toyota, Honda, Ford or BMW stated time for a coolant replacement was found: the manufacturer documents that turned up either bundle the coolant work into a larger repair, tell the dealer to use clock time (GM bulletin 25-NA-052), or cover something else (Hyundai 1.1 hr for a hybrid battery coolant loop; Karma 3.0 hr for a low-volume luxury car). Parts caveats: the two Aisin low prices are multiplied on the assumption that each is a one-gallon jug, which the pages do not print; the BMW capacity is from a reference table, not a BMW document; the BMW high figure is a retailer price for genuine coolant, not a list price. No chain-shop menu price could be loaded.
extras: A quote often adds a coolant disposal or environmental fee, shop supplies and sales tax. A machine exchange or chemical flush, a cooling system pressure test, a new radiator cap or a thermostat are common add-ons. Leaking hoses, a seeping water pump or a clogged heater core found during the service are quoted separately. Vehicles with separate cooling loops (hybrids, turbo intercooler circuits) or a vacuum-fill bleeding procedure take longer. Trucks and large engines need more coolant than the car figures here.
